title: Robert Hogarth: Will AI Force Lawyers to Raise Their Game?
author: Robert Hogarth

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the narrower claim that generative AI can produce useful legal analysis and distinguishes that output from legal advice. However, it does not address whether specialist workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration, contextual integration or human verification defend durable legal-software value, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Hogarth accepts the cluster’s core human-led, selective-deployment proposition and adds a concrete litigation workflow: AI extracts pleadings into an expected-value model while users retain control over assumptions and revisions. His acknowledgment that outputs still require judgment and supervision reinforces the cluster’s verification boundary, although his broader quality predictions rest mainly on product experience.

kp.k: AI automates settlement modelling that lawyers resisted doing
kp.d: Hogarth says Settle Index's objective over about five years has remained valuing disputes, but its implementation has changed because lawyers would not undertake financial modelling themselves. He reports that the software now creates decision trees and produces settlement valuations from uploaded pleadings, rather than requiring a lawyer to construct the model. This is the founder's account of product capabilities, not an independently measured finding.
qs: I've always been of the view that lawyers should do financial modeling when they're trying to advise clients about settlement and actually you can't get them to do it and after 5 years I've  decided you can't get them to do it.
So the software completely creates the model now. It creates the decision tree
because we can now put a value on a case by uploading pleadings.

kp.k: Language-model extraction feeds separate probability calculations
kp.d: Hogarth describes an architecture in which OpenAI extracts information from documents, while Settle Index performs probability and outcome-weighting calculations in its own software. He explains valuation as summing probability-weighted outcomes and claims the service can operate across jurisdictions and languages, requiring disputes with issues and numbers. His examples of multilingual use are informal tests rather than systematic validation.
qs: So we we pass the document to open  AI at the moment and and what that does is it extracts the information we need from it. All of the actual probabilities and waiting etc is done within our software.
you take all the value of  the outcomes weighted and add them together and that gives you your value.
It just needs a dispute which has issues and numbers and in fact it can do any language as well.

kp.d: Hogarth says he is beginning work with a law firm to compare model valuations with previously settled cases. He anticipates adjusting algorithms for the best average fit across 100 cases; no results are reported. Young suggests confidence intervals, while Hogarth proposes a possible target of settlements at or below the predicted amount in 90% of cases from the defendant's perspective. These are proposed calibration objectives, not achieved accuracy statistics.

kp.k: Automated assessments still require lawyers' review
kp.d: Hogarth strongly encourages lawyers to review generated valuations and change their parameters. Although Settle Index disclaims giving legal advice, he says it now includes approximately two pages of AI-generated legal analysis. He praises this analysis as KC-standard based on his own observations, but acknowledges odd answers and the need for judgment and supervision. These are practitioner impressions, not benchmark findings or measured hallucination rates.

kp.k: Client-facing reports can pressure lawyers toward adoption
kp.d: Hogarth describes a newly introduced public-facing service through which individuals upload pleadings and receive a free PDF report. At the time of recording, he says the first submission arrived that day from a client rather than a lawyer. He personally processes submissions, so this is not an automatic delivery service. He expects clients to bring reports to their lawyers; modifying assumptions or using additional functionality requires a subscription. Young also identifies potential feedback data for refining outcomes.

kp.k: Early modelling could reduce economically unproductive litigation
kp.d: Hogarth argues that early financial modelling grounds parties in likely settlement outcomes before they incur substantial trial-preparation costs. He suggests that both poor lawyers and highly capable lawyers pursuing clever points can impede economical resolution, and that prolonged work may barely change settlement value. Young endorses maximizing clients' net financial outcomes but notes emotional motives, tactical objectives, and inability or refusal to pay as qualifications. Hogarth treats modelling as a starting point rather than a substitute for negotiation.
qs: you've just poured money away trying to move it from 40% to 33%.
the way we run disputes in this country is you try to settle the case while all the time preparing for a very expensive trial.
modeling at the beginning gives you a grounding in realistically where you're going to end up.
some pursue litigation for emotional reasons or or for some other tactical reason unrelated to the actual dispute.
that doesn't mean you shouldn't start from the best place possible.

kp.k: Neutral valuations could support broader dispute-resolution roles
kp.d: Young proposes uses for lawyers, clients, insurers, mediators and potentially arbitrators. Hogarth suggests inserting Settle Index into contractual escalation processes before executives negotiate, describing its valuation as neutral and attentive to issues, claims and the costs of not settling. Young links predicted settlement ranges to insurance reserving, and Hogarth adds settlement itself. These are proposed applications rather than demonstrated adoption or outcomes.

because it does produce a completely  neutral evaluation. It's not on either side.
they can  choose a reserve and all sorts by reference to that.

kp.k: AI may raise standards or undermine weaker lawyers
kp.d: Young asks whether improving AI will make poor lawyering less tolerable and suggests weaker practitioners may either improve through AI support or become unable to compete. Hogarth agrees with the direction of that prediction, citing his impression that models deliver consistent quality across legal areas whereas lawyers specialize. He qualifies this with the continuing need for supervision and argues that expectations of AI perfection contrast with tolerance of human mistakes. The discussion offers no measured evidence of changes in lawyer quality or displacement.

kp.k: Confidentiality assurances depend on document and service arrangements
kp.d: Hogarth says Settle Index uses an API version of OpenAI, not a public interface, and ordinarily needs pleadings rather than confidential documents. He acknowledges that pre-action letters of claim and responses are private. Young asserts that enterprise API confidentiality promises resemble those of cloud providers and concludes there is no privilege risk. These are the speakers' assurances, not an independently established legal or security finding.

kp.k: Advice restrictions and insurance expose unresolved liability questions
kp.d: Young frames recent OpenAI developments as contractual restrictions on legal and medical advice rather than removal of model capabilities. Both speakers speculate that restrictions may be more enforceable business-to-business than against consumers; Young characterizes the change as liability-driven disclaimer drafting. Hogarth reports that his errors-and-omissions underwriters scrutinized AI use and whether Settle Index provides legal advice, with the renewal outcome still unknown. Young predicts coverage through endorsements or standalone generative-AI policies.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hogarth claims AI enables automated settlement modelling from pleadings, supplies high-quality legal analysis, and will pressure lawyers to improve; he anticipates wider use of early, neutral financial assessments to guide dispute resolution.
pts.d: Hogarth says Settle Index can now construct a decision tree and produce a settlement valuation without a lawyer building the model. He distinguishes the AI's document extraction and legal appraisal from the probabilities and weighting performed within Settle Index's own software. He describes the output as a neutral assessment incorporating issues, claims and the costs of not settling. He argues that modelling at the outset provides a realistic settlement baseline that years of litigation preparation may do little to change. He also describes OpenAI's accompanying legal analysis as comparable to King's Counsel advice and consistently strong across subject areas. Responding to the question of whether AI will force lawyers to improve, he agrees that this follows from its breadth of knowledge, while acknowledging a continuing need for judgment and supervision. He says the product is jurisdiction-agnostic and multilingual. Potential developments include incorporating it into contractual dispute-escalation processes and producing settlement estimates useful for insurers' decisions. His target that settlements fall at or below the prediction in 90% of cases is an aspiration, not an achieved accuracy rate.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally Hogarth's product-development and legal-practice experience, informal examination of outputs, and live-case testing; quantitative validation is described as forthcoming.
pts.d: Hogarth draws on approximately five years developing Settle Index and a 42-year career at RPC, including insurance and construction disputes. His account of lawyers' reluctance to model settlement values is an experience-based explanation for automating the process. He describes the underlying mathematics as the established method of summing probability-weighted outcome values, referring to Bernoulli's 1738 treatment of valuing chances. His assessment of AI legal quality rests on reading analyses generated from pleadings and recognizing cited cases; he does not report a systematic citation audit, independent quality evaluation or measured error rate. He says he has tested the software on pleadings downloaded from live court cases and has uploaded Latin cases to test language capabilities. He is only beginning a law-firm collaboration to compare model outputs with historical settlements and proposes adjusting algorithms for a best fit across 100 cases. No results, sample characteristics, held-out validation or achieved predictive accuracy are supplied. The public-upload service's first submission is a single example of client-led uptake, not evidence of adoption at scale. The prediction of improved lawyer quality and the argument that early modelling could reduce unnecessary litigation spending are supported by professional reasoning and anecdotes, not measured outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Automation and the public-report service are presented as current capabilities at the interview; validation, insurer-oriented prediction thresholds and professional improvement remain prospective and conditional.
pts.d: In the supplied 2026-labelled source, Hogarth says the move to extracting model inputs from pleadings occurred 'this year' and that the first public submission arrived 'today'; the transcript supplies no exact dates. Historical-case testing is just starting. He sets no deadline for achieving predictive thresholds or for AI raising lawyers' standards. Although model construction is automated, he explicitly requires lawyer review, permits changes to assumptions, and acknowledges occasional strange answers. Settle Index describes its output as an assessment rather than legal advice and directs users to their lawyers. The public PDF service is not an autonomous delivery workflow: Hogarth personally processes submissions and sends reports. Free reports can be viewed, but modifying the model and using additional functionality requires a subscription. The current extraction provider is OpenAI through an API. Hogarth says pleadings can supply the necessary inputs without confidential documents, but recognizes that pre-action claim letters and responses are private. His financial-modelling argument is qualified by recognition that affordability, negotiation and human behaviour can affect actual outcomes; modelling supplies a starting point rather than determining every settlement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects principally concern dispute lawyers, litigants and insurers: less manual modelling, earlier financial guidance, client-led scrutiny of advice and potentially more informed settlement decisions.
pts.d: For litigation lawyers, Hogarth describes a shift from constructing models to reviewing AI-assisted assessments and changing their parameters. He expects AI's cross-specialty knowledge to pressure professional standards, contrasting it with lawyers' narrower specialisms. For clients and members of the public, the free upload-and-report service creates a way to obtain an assessment and take it to an existing lawyer; he explicitly presents this as a route to making lawyers engage with the tool. He reports that the first submission came from a client rather than a lawyer. For litigants funding prolonged disputes, early modelling is intended to clarify likely net outcomes before substantial expenditure. Hogarth cautions that even highly skilled litigators can generate costly complexity through clever arguments. For insurers, a reliably calibrated prediction threshold could support settlement decisions, although that capability remains a goal. For businesses, he proposes using Settle Index before progressing further through contractual escalation. The claimed jurisdictional and language flexibility extends the potential market beyond England and Wales. The transcript describes free public availability but does not establish that the service has reduced unmet civil legal need.
